newsitem.title: USA: Bitter cold extends from Great Plains to deep South.
newsitem.headline: Bitter cold extends from Great Plains to deep South.

text.p: Residents huddled in bitter cold weather from the Great Plains to the deep South on Thursday while the sun broke through for the first time this week in the blizzard-hit Dakotas.
Meanwhile, motorists in parts of Alabama, Georgia and the Florida panhandle woke to find a layer of snow on their cars and sidewalks.
Warnings of icy roads that sent panicked Atlantans flocking to grocery stores late on Wednesday were unrealized after the few flakes melted by Thursday morning.
A moderately powerful storm brought a combination of wet snow and rain to the East Coast, which braced for the cold air gradually moving out of the nation's midsection.

Williston, North Dakota, was chilled to a temperature of minus 26 degrees (minus 32 Celsius) and Chicago's thermometer dipped to 3 degrees (minus 16 C), while strong winds made it feel considerably colder.

Temperatures were forecast to rise over the weekend and could climb above freezing in the plains states before the next Arctic blast arrives next week, forecaster Mike Palmerino of Weather Services Corp. said.
Blizzard conditions persisted in parts of Minnesota and Iowa, with high winds toppling a mail truck on a highway in southwestern Minnesota.

Two Indian reservations in South Dakota asked for help to clear roads and dig out snowdrifts that reached rooftops. Residents of Cheyenne River and Standing Rock reservations near the North Dakota border said cars were buried, and the snow was packed so hard it broke the blade on a snow plough.
In Kansas City, Missouri, homeless shelters overflowed with people seeking refuge.

Sandy Baldwin, a spokeswoman for the City Union Shelter, said one shelter was forced to turn away at least five families on Wednesday because it was full. She said the homeless men's shelter, which has 86 beds, accommodated 165 people by putting extra mattresses on floors.
Sub-freezing temperatures extended as far south as New Orleans and the Rio Grande in Texas, with farmers checking for damage to citrus and vegetable crops.
An elderly man died in a house fire in Fort Worth, Texas, apparently after his furniture caught fire from a wood-burning stove he may have lit to stay warm.

The cold air headed down the Florida peninsula and freeze warnings -- including the possibility of snow by Friday morning -- were posted almost as far south as Orlando. But forecasters said there was little risk Miami would have its first-ever white Christmas.
